narrative:
The model estimated a 66.8% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because the law school used that estimate in its admission screening, your application was denied; this is not a finding that you cannot succeed, but a risk score that crossed the school’s threshold.

The denial was driven mainly by two academic-history signals: your third-year class decile was the most influential factor, and your first-year class decile was second. Both pointed toward likely bar failure. Your third-year standing was 1 compared with an average of about 5.8 among accepted students, and your first-year standing was also 1 compared with an average of about 6.0. In practical terms, the model saw your classroom standing in those years as unusually different from the pattern of students who were admitted and later passed, and treated that as a strong warning sign against you.

Your undergraduate GPA was the third most important factor, and it worked in your favor: at 3.60 it was above the accepted-student average of about 3.23, pushing the prediction toward passing. It helped, but it was not enough to outweigh the two class-standing signals.

To improve your next application, ask admissions whether you can provide context for your first- and third-year rankings, such as grade trends, extenuating circumstances, or stronger later coursework. Consider retaking the LSAT, since your 31 is below the accepted average, and seek schools that review applicants holistically. A pre-law advisor can help you build a supplemental explanation and a plan to demonstrate bar-exam readiness.
